artifact.title: Batik in Indonesia: Evidence Gaps in the Provided Sources

summary:
The provided material does not establish batik’s origins in Indonesia.
It gives no evidence about regional or court traditions.
It does not document colonial-era changes to batik.
It does not confirm or describe UNESCO recognition of Indonesian batik.
It offers no account of contemporary practice.
Some sources are explicitly marked as unrelated to batik history or practice.
The UNESCO-related material describes the heritage program generally, not batik’s place in it.
No disagreements about batik can be identified from these passages.
Confidence: low; evidence is thin across every requested historical and contemporary topic.
sections: UNESCO context is general, not batik-specific

artifact.title: Borobudur Temple: Construction, Builders, and Rediscovery

summary:
The sources place Borobudur's construction broadly in the 8th century [S2].
They associate the temple with the Shailendra dynasty, which promoted Mahayana Buddhism and built Buddhist monuments in Central Java [S4].
The evidence supports a dynasty-level attribution, not the identification of a specific patron, architect, or workforce [S4].
Worldwide knowledge of the temple's existence was sparked in 1814 [S2].
Thomas Stamford Raffles, then the British administrator of Java, was advised of its location by native Indonesians [S2].
The sources do not establish that this was the first local knowledge of the temple [S2].
A separate passage links Borobudur to the Buddhist Sailendra dynasty but does not give a construction date or rediscovery account [S9].
No supplied source directly disputes the broad dating, dynasty association, or 1814 account.
Confidence: medium; evidence is thin on precise dating, named builders, and the details of the rediscovery.
sections: The Shailendra dynasty is associated with the temple
Raffles was informed of its location in 1814
The additional dynasty reference is contextual
